overview: This bill, the EQUALS Act, changes the probation period for new federal employees. Today most new civil servants serve one year before gaining full job protections; the bill makes it two years (one year for veterans with hiring preference) and applies a similar two-year trial period to "excepted service" jobs, which are positions filled outside the standard competitive hiring process. Under the bill, a probationary employee is automatically let go at the end of the period unless the agency certifies to the Office of Personnel Management, the government's HR agency, that keeping the person serves the public interest. It also lengthens the time before employees can appeal firings or other serious discipline to match the new periods, and extends the rules to Veterans Affairs medical staff and to the FAA and TSA, while exempting Postal Service and congressional employees. Most changes would apply to people hired starting one year after the bill becomes law. As of April 9, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar.
for: Supporters say a longer probation and an active decision to keep each new hire give managers enough time to judge performance and make it easier to keep only effective workers in permanent federal jobs.
against: Critics say automatic termination unless an agency acts could cost good employees their jobs through paperwork lapses, and that delaying appeal rights leaves new workers more exposed to arbitrary or politically motivated firings.
